task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to measure similarity of initiation profiles between an absent player and teammates?
How to define and measure 'largest gainer' in the absent player's primary play types?
What is the adequate sample size (spells, players) to detect a meaningful correlation between similarity and usage gain?
How to control for confounding factors such as role, opponent, game context, and coaching decisions?
How to handle regression to the mean when the absent player is an outlier in their primary types?
How to deal with sparse pre-absence baseline for teammates in the absent player's primary types?
evidence_establishes: No historical evidence was available from prior project studies on this specific question.
own_inferences: The research question is a plausible hypothesis about offensive reorganization, but it is very demanding of data and measurement precision.
The available sample of only 11 cases (likely unique absent-player primary-type profiles, or qualifying spells) is far too small for a reliable test, even if 148 spells are recorded.
Defining 'closest pre-absence initiation profile' involves many researcher degrees of freedom (distance metric, features, normalization), which risks overfitting and false positives.

The outcome 'largest gainer in the absent player's primary types' can be dominated by regression-to-the-mean and floor effects, especially for teammates with little pre-absence involvement in those types.
Multiple definitions of similarity (minutes, initiations, same-position minutes, profile) amount to multiple comparisons and would require pre-registration and correction.
uncertainties: The exact meaning of 'n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases' is ambiguous. It could be 148 absence spells collapsed into 11 independent cases (e.g., players), which would severely limit statistical power.
The reliability of derived play-type possession records from [source] database is not reported; misclassification could bias findings.

It is unclear whether the data contain enough instances of absences where (a) the absent player has a clear set of primary play types and (b) at least one teammate has a comparable initiation profile.
The time frame (three seasons, partial fourth) may not provide a stable tactical environment; team systems and player roles change.

historical_effect.explanation: No earlier study was retrieved, so the decision is based solely on the current task statement and methodological assessment.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 11 cases (likely independent units) are recorded; effect sizes for similarity-gain correlations in this setting are likely small, leading to extremely low power.
The absent player's primary play types may occur infrequently, and most teammates may have zero or very few pre-absence initiations in those types, making gain estimates unreliable.

prior_work.summary: No prior work on this specific hypothesis was retrieved from the project's study-family records.

risks.text: With only 11 cases, the study would be severely underpowered to detect a plausible effect size, even using all 148 spells if those are nested within 11 independent units.
Pre-absence initiation counts in the absent player's primary types are likely zero for many teammates, causing floor effects and inflating relative gains artificially.
Play-type classification from [source] database may contain errors; 'initiation profile' similarity depends heavily on the chosen distance metric and feature weighting, with no validated standard.

The absent player is typically an extreme user of their primary play types; teammates with the most similar profile may still be far from the extreme, and their usage increase may partly reflect regression to the team mean.

Opponent defensive schemes, score differential, coaching adjustments, and simultaneous absences of other players all influence play-calling and are not easily controlled in a small observational sample.

The question suggests testing several similarity definitions (profile, minutes, initiations, same-position minutes), inflating the risk of a false positive unless multiplicity correction is pre-registered.
Teammates who never initiated a play type pre-absence can only stay the same or increase; this asymmetry biases upward their observed gain relative to teammates who already had some involvement.
Incorrect assignment of initiator or play type in the derived possession records could misclassify both the absent player's primary types and the teammate's gains.

design.estimand: The correlation (or rank agreement) between a teammate's similarity to the absent player in pre-absence initiation profile and that teammate's absolute (or relative) increase in usage of the absent player's primary play types during the absence spell.
design.unit: One absence spell (consecutive games missed by a single player due to injury/rest).
design.sample: All spells where: (a) the absent player missed at least 4 games, (b) the absent player had a 'primary play type' defined as any type they initiated at least 2 times per game and that constitutes at least 15% of their total initiations, (c) at least three teammates played >10 minutes per game pre-absence, and (d) no other starter missed more than 2 games in the same spell. This would filter to an even smaller set than 11 cases.
design.power: A Taylor-series power analysis assuming a true Spearman rank correlation of 0.3 across spells (with spells as independent unit) would require >200 spells after filtering for 80% power. The current dataset falls far short.
design.controls: Team fixed effects, game location, opponent defensive rating, number of days since last game, and pre-absence teammate usage in those same play types (to separate floor effects).
design.falsification: Test whether the predicted largest gainer also shows a disproportionate increase in play types that are not primary for the absent player; if the same teammate gains everywhere, the effect is likely driven by role, not profile similarity.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single similarity metric based on a hold-out season; if multiple are explored, apply Bonferroni correction and report all.
design.decision_rule: The hypothesis is considered supported if the pre-registered similarity metric shows a statistically significant positive coefficient (p<0.05, one-sided) in a mixed-effects model predicting gain in primary-type usage, with the falsification check non-significant and the effect size at least a pre-defined minimum (e.g., 0.2 standard deviations in gain per standard deviation of similarity).
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season and playoffs, per-game play-by-play and derived play-type possessions as of 2026-11-01.
